title: More, longer, more diverse realistic fluid sims: viscosity variants and color mixing on the GPU renderer
objective: Build a longer, more diverse, more capable set of realistic fluid animations on top of the fast GPU screen-space renderer (sim/fluid_render_gpu.py), following up improve-basic-fluid-sim-realism whose clips were too short and too few. Deliver several distinct starting conditions (a faucet filling a tank, multiple colored drops, a dam-break column collapse, a thick honey pour, two converging faucets, two colliding jets), at least one thin water-like and one thick honey-like viscosity, and the standout: per-particle color so two dyed liquids visibly blend where they meet. Every clip must be much longer than the prior two-second animations. All new code lives in a fresh module (sim/fluid_showcase_gpu.py) that imports the GPU renderer, an emitter-capable MLS-MPM fluid with the Newtonian viscous stress reused from sim/fluid_viscosity.py, and a color-aware renderer subclass; none of the committed shared files are mutated. Graded on how the images look and on honest scope; no claim of physical light transport, real diffusion, differentiability, or real-time performance.
findings: Six scenes were produced, each rendered on the GPU color renderer at 1000x1000, every clip between 11 and 14 seconds of playback (water_pour 13 s, triple_drop 12 s, dam_break 11 s, jet_collide 11 s, color_faucets 14 s, honey_coil a 12 s clip of 6.5 s of physics at 1.85x slow motion), a large step up from the roughly two-second prior clips. Length is now cheap because the render is a one-to-two-second GPU job, so the constraint moved to the simulation, and sustained motion over ten-plus seconds needs sustained forcing: a single release in a closed box goes quiet within about a second, so the faucet, jet and drop scenes use emitters that keep feeding fresh fluid, spreading each frame's birth batch along the flow so a stream reads as a continuous ribbon. Two viscosities are shown against the same pipeline: the water scenes use a thin Newtonian strain-rate stress (mu_visc 0.03-0.04) that also drains grid-scale velocity noise, and honey_coil uses mu_visc = 0.5 (a hundredfold thicker) with a softer stiffness (E = 200) and a much smaller timestep (dt = 1.5e-5) for the explicit-viscosity stability limit; the honey buckles and coils into a mound that holds its shape, the classic high-viscosity signature, where the thin water splashes and settles flat. The standout is per-particle color, added to the GPU pipeline without mutating it: each particle carries an RGB dye set once at birth and never read by the physics, atomic-scattered per channel into GPU fields, blurred, and divided by the particle count blurred at the same width to give a smooth local mean hue that drives the Beer-Lambert body tint in place of the single fixed water color. The color field is deliberately blurred wider than the density mask (2.5 times the density sigma) so an interface between two dyes reads as a soft blend band rather than a razor seam, and the count denominator is blurred at that same wider width so the ratio stays a valid local mean and pure regions keep their source hue. color_faucets pours red and blue together, angled inward and swept slowly side to side so the streams interleave, and blends to a clear purple band down the middle while red and blue stay legible on their sides; triple_drop drops red, green, blue and yellow dollops in sequence into a shallow pool that marbles at soft color transitions; jet_collide fires red and yellow jets together (chosen so their average is a clean orange rather than the muddy grey a near-complementary pair averages to) and grows an orange confluence band. Every clip was viewed at early, middle and late frames: all six stayed finite with peak speeds between 3.2 and 4.4, no interior holes appeared at any point, and none drifted or blew up over the long rollout (up to about 56000 particles and roughly 175000 to 430000 substeps per scene).
hypothesis: Two mechanisms explain what is seen. First, the color behaves as a textbook passive tracer: a Lagrangian particle keeps its identity for the whole simulation, so attaching a color to a particle advects it for free, and where two colored populations interleave the renderer's local average lands at an intermediate hue. This is why the blend is purely geometric, decided by where the flow carries the particles, and why it never feeds back into the dynamics. Second, and important for honesty, an equal-density, non-diffusive weakly-compressible fluid does not homogenise: with no molecular diffusion and a pressure that resists interpenetration, two dyed bodies tend to stratify at a sharp interface rather than dissolve into each other, so the raw particle mix stays close to a moving seam. The visible blend therefore comes from two deliberate choices: stirring the interface (converging, swept faucets; colliding jets; overlapping drop crowns) so the resolved flow folds the two populations together, and blurring the color field wider than the density at render time so a thin interleaved zone reads as a smooth blend band of the width set by that blur. Turn the color blur up and the band widens toward a uniform muddy tone; turn it down and the seam sharpens; matched a little above the density blur it gives a legible blend that keeps the source colors. The honey result follows from the added stress being proportional to the strain rate: it drains kinetic energy from shear, so a thick fluid converts less of its fall into spreading and instead coils and mounds, and the same term seen numerically forces the small timestep (explicit diffusion is stable only when a parcel diffuses less than about a cell per step, dt <= rho dx^2 / mu_visc). What would test generality: a genuine diffusion or reaction term for real mixing chemistry, a resolution sweep to check the blend is not purely a render-blur artefact, three-dimensional flows where vortex stretching stirs far more vigorously, and a calibrated mapping from mu_visc to a physical viscosity. The claims here are scoped to these six 2D side-view scenes at one grid resolution and one hand-tuned look.
limitations: Still a stylized 2D side-view render graded on how it looks, not physical light transport, and the color is passive advection, not real mixing. A particle's dye is constant and never crosses the interface, so at infinite resolution the blend would resolve back into interleaved source colors rather than a true continuum of intermediate concentration; the smooth blend seen here is spatial interleaving by the resolved flow plus a render-time local average whose blur width is chosen by eye. There is no molecular diffusion, no surface tension, no reaction chemistry. Because the fluid is equal-density and non-diffusive, the two-color scenes tend to stratify, so the mix reads as a soft blend band at a stirred confluence, not full homogenisation, and the specific dye pairs were chosen so their average is a clean secondary (red plus blue to purple, red plus yellow to orange) rather than the muddy grey that near-complementary pairs give. Every color, the deep and thin tint mapping, the color and density blur widths, the foam thresholds, the absorption, and the emitter rates, sweeps and geometry are hand-tuned for legibility. The fluid is a weakly-compressible MLS-MPM fluid at n_grid = 128, f32, with pure-APIC or small-FLIP transfers and a thin stabilising viscosity even on the water scenes; different settings give different splash shapes, and the narrow closed domain lets an energetic scene climb the walls and, for the faucet scenes, eventually fill the tank. Honey is shown in mild slow motion and is thick-but-finite: explicit viscosity caps how thick the fluid can go before the timestep becomes impractical. GPU atomic-add accumulation is not bitwise reproducible, so exact splash geometry drifts run to run. No gradients, loss, or optimisation anywhere; the renderer and sim are deliberately non-differentiable and offline.

results.caption: Color-mixing hero, 14 seconds. A red faucet and a blue faucet, angled toward each other and swept slowly side to side, pour together into one tank. Each particle keeps its dye for the whole run, so the falling streams stay legibly red and blue, and where the two populations interleave a soft purple blend band grows down the middle, with purple tendrils curling into the lower pool. The source colors stay clearly red and blue on their own sides; the mix reads as a blend, not a razor seam and not a grey wash. The dye is passive: the physics never reads a particle's color.

Hero still from the two-faucet color mix. Red on the left, blue on the right, and a purple confluence band where the swept streams meet, with a purple tendril folded into the lower centre. The body is a single continuous depth-shaded volume with no interior holes.

Multi-color drops, 12 seconds. Four dyed dollops (red, green, blue, yellow) are dropped in sequence into a shallow clear pool, a splash landing every few seconds. Each impact throws a colored crown and spreads laterally into its neighbours, so the pool becomes a marbled band where adjacent colors blend at soft transitions while each dollop's own hue stays legible. A distinct starting condition (discrete drops) from the continuous faucets.

Hero still from the multi-color drops: the blue (third) dollop falls into a splash crown over a pool already marbled red, green and blue from the earlier impacts. Soft color transitions where the crowns overlapped, no interior holes.

Opposing jets, 11 seconds. A red jet from the left and a yellow jet from the right fire horizontally, collide mid-air into a fan of spray, and rain down into a pool. Red and yellow are chosen because their average is a clean vivid orange (near-complementary dyes would blend to a muddy grey), so an orange blend band forms where the two liquids meet. A distinct jet/stream starting condition plus mixing.

Hero still from the opposing jets: red left, yellow right, an orange blend band down the middle, with a few colored droplets still in the air from the collision. Continuous solid body, no interior holes.

Thin water faucet filling a tank, 13 seconds. A single blue water stream falls, punches the surface, and fills the tank while the pool rises and settles. Thin viscosity (a strain-rate stress at a small coefficient) keeps it water-like and drains grid-scale noise over the long rollout. The falling stream and the pooled water are one continuous glassy translucent body that refracts the studio background, with no interior holes at any point in the fill.
Hero still from the water fill: the blue stream plunging into the rising pool, glassy and depth-graded, the structured background bending through the body.

Thick honey pour, a 12 second clip of 6.5 seconds of physics shown at 1.85x slow motion. A faucet pours a slow amber rope of honey that buckles and coils onto the floor, piling into a mound that holds its shape. The thick case uses a Newtonian viscous stress at a hundred times the water coefficient (mu_visc = 0.5) with a softer stiffness and a much smaller timestep for the explicit-viscosity stability limit. The coiling and mounding are the visible signature of high viscosity against the same realistic pipeline as the thin scenes.
Hero still from the honey pour: a buckling amber rope descending into a rounded pile it holds far longer than water would, the coil the classic tell of a thick fluid.

Dam-break, 11 seconds. A tall water column released against the left wall collapses into a fast wedge that races across the floor, runs up the far wall, and returns, sloshing back and forth before settling. Run long enough that the whole collapse-and-settle plays out; the body stays a continuous depth-graded volume with no interior holes and does not drift or blow up over the long rollout.
Hero still from the dam-break, early in the collapse: the released column has become a wedge racing across the floor, a clean continuous front with a bright grazing waterline.
